content.summary_of_the_paper:
Machine learning tasks on proteins takes as input a single conformer of the protein which is represented as a set of coordinates of the atoms.
The authors treat this as a point cloud and propose a method which is akin to a GNN on a $k$-nearest neighbor graph constructed using these co-ordinates.
They ensure rotation and translation invariance by learning a canonical ordering of the input conformer given the input protein.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths
- I love the fact that the authors incorporated the related works with the introduction which frames the problem very well and makes for concise reading.
- The idea is straightforward and well motivated. The experimental results have some issues mentioned in the next subsection but show superior performance compared to considered baselines. The authors may be able to show that using a simple model can get results comparable to or better than other SOTA methods which are complicated to implement and take more time to train due to their complexity.
- While the choice of ensuring invariance -- via learning a canonical ordering -- is non-traditional, I am interested in knowing the reasoning behind this design choice. If it does indeed perform better than a data augmentation like approach as proposed in [Janossy Pooling](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.01900) it would be an interesting step in understanding protein ML models better.

### Weaknesses
- **Experimental Evaluation:** I have some concerns regarding the choice of baselines and evaluation. Specifically all the tables lack confidence intervals and SOTA models that are rotation/translation invariant such as [GVP-GNNs](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2009.01411.pdf) and [E(n) GNNs](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.09844.pdf).
- **Invariance via Canonical Representation:**  Section 3.2
Authors seem to be learning a canonical rotation and translation of an input via an MLP. [Janossy Pooling](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.01900) expresses concerns about using a canonical ordering to achieve invariance and recommends learning it via a sum over all conformers (in this context) that you want to be invariant to. The work will benefit from a better justification for why you chose one method over the other.
Reasoning for why other design choices for rotation and translation invariance such as [SE(3) Transformers](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.10503.pdf) would help the paper as well.
- **Clarity in presentation:** 
	- In the last line of Section 2: `Usually, g can be .... or other symmetric operations`, despite writing this as invariance later on why is a less precise term (symmetric) introduced? Could you cite prior work such as [Deepsets](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06114) for the examples of invariant functions?
	- In Def 3.1, 3.2 and Lemma 3.1 I believe permutation invariant and equivariant are appropriate adjectives for $\mathcal{A}$. I.e. it should be `the operation $\mathcal{A} \colon \ldots$ is permutation equivariant if...`
	- In table 1 could you please add citations along with model to alleviate the confusion caused by multiple acronyms.
	- I did not understand the transition from equations 3, 4 and 5. Specifically Eq 4 doesn't seem to have an LHS. 
	- In Eq 2 you pass the actual co-ordinates into the NN, what happens when you translate the molecule? or flip it? Is your model to learn the canonical orientation powerful enough to transform the atom back? Is this something you tested -- rotating and translating the test data to test if your model performance is still good? (Apologies if I missed this.)
	- I wasn't able to find the definition of $h_\Theta$ after equation (2) is it invariant to the ordering of inputs? i.e. is $h(x_i, x_j) = h(x_j, x_i)$?
	- Eq 7 what is the center atom? Did I miss this definition?
	- Right after Eq 7: `~~The~~ To alleviate the problem of vanishing gradient in deep neural networks, `
	- Eq 8, what is $h_\Omega$?
	- Eq 2: You use an average since your implicit graph is $k$-regular, could you please consider average since that will make your architecture more general.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- **Clarity and Reproducibility:** Covered in weaknesses, the paper needs significant work to improve clarity of presentation, many equations are not understandable by me in their current state and design choices need better motivation. This harms reproducibility directly.
- **Quality and Novelty:** Due to the experimental evaluation, the paper's quality and novelty suffers. As detailed above, the paper needs better justification of design choices and consequently needs to be evaluated against other existing models to make its novelty clearer.
content.summary_of_the_review:
- Due to my concerns regarding the clarity, quality, novelty and reproducibility as detailed in the above section I would recommend a reject.
- The paper is interesting and can definitely be improved to the point of acceptance with effort which I believe is not possible in the author-reviewer engagement period.
- Due to my concerns about the experimental evaluation I have to say `not applicable` for the `Empirical Novelty And Significance` question since I am unsure how the method would perform against the better tailored baselines.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a neural network that uses the rdkit or Omega generated 3D conformers to predict a molecular property. The paper also benchmarks certain point-cloud methods and SchNet on a selection of tasks for property prediction of small molecules.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
This paper is confusing and at times it is poorly written and parses incorrectly (p.5 "The alleviate the problem..."). Perhaps unintentionally, the paper appears to ignore or summarily sidestep all the relevant efforts by the community to evaluate interatomic forces, energies, quantum mechanical properties from 3D coordinates of small molecules, and the additional exploding literature about the generation of 3D coordinates of small molecules from their graph. The key idea of this work is to use a 3D representation from Omega or rdkit, which in part due to their connection to QM-related properties, were already used for a number of years in practical property-prediction applications within the industry.  How would the method proposed in this paper compare in public benchmarks, or open competitions, for example the open-graph benchmark, and, importantly, how would it perform on the large-scale challenge for small molecules (PCQM4Mv2) which can help deconvolve the importance of 3D representations in prediction of properties?

The attempt to rationalize the inferiority in the solubility test is also confusing.  The number I see in the 2021 paper "Pushing the limits of solubility prediction via quality-oriented data selection" is 0.397 or 0.348, so not sure why the table 3 lists 0.559 as the MAE.  (Similarly, the R2 was 0.93 and 0.94 in that paper, not 0.872).

Finally, I have no clue what the table 4 results mean.  It is impossible for me to believe that 1.555A is relatively small for a difference in two conformations of small molecules---did the author try to visualize any of these examples and see what an RMSD of 1.6A looks like?  The RMSD of 43A or higher are meaningless in my opinion, so there is a bug somewhere.  These molecules are probably not aligned or have no meaningful geometric structure to speak of.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I do not believe that the paper as written is convincing enough of its quality.  The lack of clarity on certain benchmark choices, quoted numbers, or interpretation of results makes the paper harder to read. I am not sure if this work has a main original contribution, except possibly for the 3D molecule alignment layer, however, the results mentioned in table 4 seem to confuse the issue, so I am not sure that this idea works. The authors provide code, however I have not tried to run it or find the bugs that lead to the results in table 4.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper has enough confusing, missing, and incorrect parts to make it unsuitable for ICLR2023.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes to leverage point cloud methods, e.g., PointNet and DGCNN, for 3D molecular representation learning (MRL).  Compared to the two point-cloud-based methods, the proposed method integrates self-attention and multiple atom features. In addition,  transformation invariance techniques are added.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strength

I. Treating molecules as point clouds is technically sound and reasonable.

II.  The proposed method outperforms most state-of-the-art on both classification and regression tasks.

III. The code is provided. 

# Weaknesses

I. The main novety or significant motivation or difference is not very clear.
1. To my understanding, the main or principle operation of the work is Eq. (2), which is based on local structure modeling, self-attention and center-neighbor-feature concatenation. However, these or similar strategies have been widely used in point cloud processing. For example, Point Transformer [1] combines local structure modeling and self-attention. FlowNet3D [2] concatenates  center and its neighbors' features. Moreover, for feature processing, the method in FlowNet3D, which concatenates displacements and center and neighbors' features, may be more reasonable.  There are also many existing works to address the rotation problem in point clouds, such as [3],[4] and [5]. Finally, this operation is more like an extension of Transformer. 

       [1] Point Transformer. Zhao et al. ICCV 2021.

       [2] FlowNet3D: Learning Scene Flow in 3D Point Clouds. Liu et al. CVPR 2019.

       [3] Tensor field networks: Rotation- and translation-equivariant neural networks for 3D point clouds. Thomas et al. Arxiv 2018.

       [4] Rotation Invariant Convolutions for 3D Point Clouds Deep Learning. Zhang et al. 3DV 2019.

       [5] A Closer Look at Rotation-invariant Deep Point Cloud Analysis. Li et al. ICCV 2021.

2. The motivation to employ self-attention or Transformer is not clear.  When using self-attention, one may want to find the relation, relevance or semantic similarity between two points. However, in molecular representation learning, what do you want self-attention to learn besides distance? 
I think some visualizations of self-attention maps may help. 

II. The method treats the atomic interaction information (e.g., covalent bonds and non-covalent interactions) as atom attributes, which is not that reasonable. If we visualize a molecule, we can find that bonds provide important visual cues for recognition.  Treating them as atom attributes may increase the challenge to networks for molecule modeling. 

III. Since the method treats the atomic interaction information as point attributes or features, the method can also be used to pure point clouds or colourful point clouds, by slightly changing or removing additional "atom" attributes.  In this case, it could be interesting to see the accuracy on point cloud tasks, such as shape classification or object segmentation. 

IV. PointNet and DGCNN are only two simple methods for point cloud understanding. Comparison with more powerful methods, such as PointNet++[6], Point Transfromer [1] or PointMLP [6], are missing. Moreover, when compared with point cloud methods, the atom attributes/features and rotation invariant techniques should be also used. Otherwise, it cannot prove the effectiveness of Eq. (2). Also, the analysis for model size, i.e., the number of parameters, is missing.

[6] PointNet++: Deep Hierarchical Feature Learning on Point Sets in a Metric Space. Qi et al. NeurIPS 2017.

[7] Rethinking Network Design and Local Geometry in Point Cloud: A Simple Residual MLP Framework. Ma et al. ICLR 2022. 

V. A few key ablation studies are missing. They are about self-attention, feature concatenation,  transformation invariance and atom attributes. Without these ablation studies, it is not clear whether the proposed method is really better than existing point cloud methods.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I can understand the main idea of the paper but not all the details.  The good thing is that the code is provided. Thank the authors.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I like the idea that using point cloud methods to address molecular representation learning. However, there are not too many significant differences compared to existing point cloud methods.  Some components, such as self-attention, are not well-motivated. The way to exploit the atomic interaction information is not very reasonable or at least not the best one. Finally, a few experiments and comparisons are missing.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a method for 3D molecule pretraining. However, from the current draft, the motivation and the contribution of this paper are not clear.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Weaknesses:

1. The definition of "point-based" is very confusing. Authors only classify the "SchNet" to this class, while I believe the "DimeNet", and "SphereNet" are also based on 3D positions, why they are classified as "graph-based"? Besides, the proposed method itself is a graph model, which uses k-nearest atoms as neighbors. 
2. The motivation is unclear. 
   - "However, the SchNet model does not explicitly utilize the coordinates of atoms, and neglected the direction of atomic interactions, which contains important information about the bond angles and the topology of molecular substructures." Why SchNet "does not explicitly utilize the coordinates of atoms"? What is "direction of atomic interactions"? How the proposed method addresses the problem? 
3. Why are "pointNet" and "DGCNN" better?
4. "scaled dot-product attention satisfies the principle of permutation invariance" is a piece of common knowledge, I don't think author need to prove it in the main paper.
5. I cannot understand eq(9), in which there is a max, then softmax? Which dimensions are max/softmax applied on? Why does the output need to be normalized by softmax? 
6. It seems the "TnRNet" learns a global rotation and translation for all points. If I didn't misunderstand, "TnRNet" is used for the data augmentation, to provide transformed 3D inputs. Why not use random rotations and translations?
7. Many baselines, like Grover and GEM, are missed in the experiments.
8. The novelty of the proposed method is not clear, largely based on previous work.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Referring to the "Weaknesses", the Clarity, Quality, and Novelty of this paper are poor in its current form.
content.summary_of_the_review: Due to the poor clarity and quality, I recommend the rejection.

content.title: Point-based Molecular Representation Learning from Conformers
content.TL;DR: This paper proposes a point-based deep network for molecular representation learning from three-dimensional conformers.
content.abstract: Molecular representation learning (MRL) aims to embed molecules into vectors in a high dimensional latent space, which can be used (and reused) for the prediction of various molecular properties. Most current MRL models exploited the SMILES (Simplified Molecular-Input Line-Entry System) strings or molecular graphs as the input format of molecules. As a result, these methods may not capture the full information encoded in the three-dimensional (3D) molecular conformations (also known as the conformers). With mature algorithms for generating 3D molecular conformers, we propose to engage the abundant geometric information in the molecular conformers by representing molecules as point sets, and adapt the point-based deep neural network for MRL. Specifically, we designed an atom-shared elemental operation that extracts features from individual atoms as well as atomic interactions (including covalent bonds and non-covalent interactions), and a mini-network that ensures the representation invariant to rotations and translations of the molecular conformers. We trained the deep neural network (referred to as Mol3DNet) for a variety of tasks of molecular properties prediction using benchmarking datasets. The experimental results demonstrated that Mol3DNet achieves state-of-the-art performance on these classification and regression tasks, except for one task (solubility prediction) where all deep learning models underperform a customized machine learning model.
